The system automatically analyses village-level planning and spending records — development plans, sanctions, payments, works and photo evidence from Gram Panchayats, blocks, and districts — and surfaces patterns worth an official's attention. The current data is a 20-Gram-Panchayat sample; percentages describe the sample, not the state.

Your readers are busy block-, district- and state-level officials, not data analysts. They read these insights to decide where to direct attention: which districts to question, which records to reconcile, which local practices to check at the next review.

Below are findings from the analysis engine, each written in the engine's internal style — accurate but full of database language — along with reference figures for each. Rewrite each finding as an insight a senior officer would find clear and actionable:

- a one-to-two-sentence lead the officer sees first. This should be interesting enough to catch a reader's attention and easy enough to understand that the officer doesn't need to read the subsequent paragraph simply to understand it. Lead with what the officer would act on — usually the size and direction of the issue — rather than with the statistical pattern.
- a short detail paragraph explaining what was found, which places are exceptions and in what way, and what is worth checking or asking at the next review.

Write naturally, in plain English. Use the reference figures where they strengthen the point; use no number that is not provided. Be direct about what the data can and cannot establish — an insight that overstates certainty could send an official after the wrong problem.

Give your answer for each finding below, in order. Delimit each one exactly like this:

===FINDING 1===
LEAD: <the lead>
DETAIL: <the detail paragraph>
===FINDING 2===
LEAD: ...
DETAIL: ...

...and so on, one block per finding.

response_text:
===FINDING 1===
LEAD: The 20 sampled Gram Panchayats spent ₹51.96 crore less than planned on costed activities, with the gap spread across blocks and almost every asset category. Rangeilunda and Kalimela warrant first attention, with shortfalls of ₹9.11 crore and ₹5.90 crore respectively.
DETAIL: Across 5,630 costed activities, no single block drove the shortfall in 27 of the 28 recorded asset categories. Rangeilunda spent ₹2.73 crore of ₹11.84 crore planned and Kalimela ₹1.76 crore of ₹7.65 crore—about 23% utilisation in each; no clear distribution pattern was found for Banking Facilities. At the next review, ask these blocks to reconcile plans with expenditure records and identify delayed, cancelled or incomplete works; the data shows a spending gap but cannot establish whether it reflects implementation delays, changed plans or missing expenditure entries.

===FINDING 1===
LEAD: The 20-GP sample records spending of Rs 51.96 crore below plan across 5,630 costed activities, and the gap is widespread rather than driven by one block. Rangeilunda and Kalimela have the largest block-level gaps, at Rs 9.11 crore and Rs 5.90 crore respectively.
DETAIL: In 27 of 28 asset categories, the plan–spending gap is distributed across the 16 sampled blocks rather than concentrated in one place. Banking Facilities did not show the same pattern, but the data provide no clear alternative explanation. Blocks should review ageing costed activities and reconcile plans, progress and payments, with early attention to Rangeilunda and Kalimela; the figures show recorded underspending, not why it occurred.
===FINDING 4===
LEAD: For activities with sanctions on file, recorded spending is Rs 5.02 crore below the sanctioned amount across the nine sampled districts. Ganjam has the largest gap at Rs 1.68 crore, followed by Khordha at Rs 73.70 lakh.
DETAIL: The shortfall is spread across districts in 27 of 28 asset categories, so it is not attributable to a single district or asset type; Banking Facilities has no clear pattern. Ganjam spent Rs 4.61 crore of Rs 6.30 crore sanctioned, while Khordha spent Rs 3.33 crore of Rs 4.06 crore. These figures cover only activities with a sanction record—about one in six—so districts should reconcile sanction, payment and progress records rather than treat them as programme-wide utilisation rates.
===FINDING 5===
LEAD: Codes 101 and 105 account for Rs 51.78 crore, or 92.2%, of planned untied funding for public works in the sample. This concentration appears in 19 of the 20 Gram Panchayats.
DETAIL: Code 101 holds Rs 34.88 crore and Code 105 Rs 16.90 crore of the Rs 56.20 crore total; Haldikudar follows a different pattern. Because none of the output-type codes has a description on file, officials cannot tell from these records what this concentration represents. The code definitions should be restored and Haldikudar’s classification checked before drawing conclusions about local priorities.
===FINDING 7===
LEAD: More than half of public works—5,181 of 9,418, or 55.0%—have no asset category recorded. “Uncategorised” is the largest group in 19 of the 20 sampled Gram Panchayats.
DETAIL: Govindapur is the only GP with a different pattern. Buildings, the largest named category, accounts for just 688 activities, compared with 5,181 lacking a category. Blocks should require the missing asset categories to be completed, starting with older or higher-value works, so that investment and delivery can be reviewed reliably by asset type.
===FINDING 8===
LEAD: Activities still recorded as “Activity Approved” account for Rs 41.61 crore of the sample’s Rs 51.96 crore gap between planned cost and spending. Only Rs 14.00 lakh is recorded as spent against their Rs 41.75 crore planned cost.
DETAIL: This is the largest status-level gap in 18 of the 20 GPs; Boipariguda and Laxmipur show no clear pattern. “Activity Approved” also covers 53.9% of costed activities, while abandoned works show a further Rs 5.64 crore gap. Review the age and actual stage of approved and abandoned works, and reconcile stale statuses, payments and closures; the records alone do not distinguish genuine non-starts from delayed updates.
===FINDING 10===
LEAD: Rs 28.59 crore, or 93.9%, of voucher-linked General-category spending on costed activities is attached to works still recorded as ongoing. This pattern holds in 18 of the 20 sampled GPs.
DETAIL: Boipariguda and Laxmipur show no clear pattern. A further Rs 1.15 crore is attached to abandoned works, while Rs 32.74 lakh is attached to “Activity Approved” and Rs 13.04 lakh to “Under Approval.” Blocks should check whether work statuses are being updated promptly and examine spending against abandoned or not-yet-approved records; these figures cover only the General social-category component.
===FINDING 12===
LEAD: Of the expected beneficiaries recorded in the sample, 2,03,534 people—or 98.4%—are attached to activities still marked “Activity Approved.” Very few recorded beneficiaries are linked to ongoing or abandoned activities.
DETAIL: The same pattern appears in 18 of 20 GPs; Boipariguda and Laxmipur have no clear pattern. Beneficiary figures are available only for the 763 activities carrying community-service details, so this is not a count of all people reached. Review whether beneficiary estimates and activity statuses are being carried forward or updated consistently, especially for older approved activities.
===FINDING 13===
LEAD: Half of planned untied funding for costed activities—Rs 30.07 crore, or 50.4%—is assigned to Theme 6, “Self-sufficient Infrastructure in Village.” It is the leading theme in 18 of the 20 sampled GPs.
DETAIL: Kalimela instead gives the largest share to Theme 4, “Water Sufficient Village,” while Boipariguda’s largest amount falls under “Unmapped theme.” Across the sample, Rs 5.70 crore is unmapped. Review whether the concentration reflects GP priorities, and correct missing theme mappings in Boipariguda and elsewhere before comparing thematic allocations.
===FINDING 14===
LEAD: Code 101 accounts for Rs 2.49 crore of the total Rs 2.54 crore gap between sanctions and spending for new works. It has the largest absolute unspent sanctioned amount in 19 of the 20 sampled GPs.
DETAIL: Chikilli shows no clear pattern. Code 101 records Rs 14.94 crore spent against Rs 17.43 crore sanctioned, or 85.7%; however, output-type descriptions are missing, so the underlying work type cannot be identified. This analysis also covers only activities with sanction records—about one in six—so officials should restore the code descriptions and reconcile the affected sanctions before assessing performance.
===FINDING 15===
LEAD: Every geotagged photo recorded for new works in this view—6,893 uploads—is attached to Code 101, although that code covers only 32.8% of new-work activities. No photos are recorded against the other four output codes shown.
DETAIL: Code 101 dominates photo uploads in 19 of 20 GPs; Chikilli has no clear pattern. This may reflect the evidence workflow, missing uploads or incorrect output coding, and the absent code descriptions prevent a firm conclusion. Check whether works under Codes 102, 103, 109 and 110 require photo evidence and whether their uploads are being attached to the correct records.
===FINDING 17===
LEAD: Codes 101 and 105 account for Rs 46.08 crore of the sample’s Rs 51.96 crore gap between planned cost and spending. The same two codes have the largest gaps across all four recorded beneficiary-purpose groups.
DETAIL: Code 101 records Rs 15.88 crore spent against Rs 46.85 crore planned, while Code 105 records Rs 7.32 crore against Rs 22.43 crore. Because the output codes have no descriptions on file, the data cannot show which kinds of activity are driving these gaps. Restore the code definitions and then review ageing, progress and payment records under Codes 101 and 105.
===FINDING 18===
LEAD: Drinking water and sanitation together receive Rs 17.24 crore, or 97.6%, of all planned tied funding for costed activities in the sample. They lead across every recorded beneficiary-purpose group.
DETAIL: Sanitation accounts for Rs 8.82 crore and drinking water Rs 8.42 crore of the Rs 17.66 crore total; roads are a distant third at Rs 31.01 lakh. This concentration may be consistent with the earmarked purpose of tied grants and does not by itself indicate a problem. Reviews should confirm that focus-area coding and proposed works match the permitted uses of the tied funds.
===FINDING 19===
LEAD: Chikilli has no sanctioned amount recorded in any of the six years from 2020-21 to 2025-26, despite accounting for 5.0% of activities in the sample. This is a strong record-reconciliation priority.
DETAIL: Chikilli is the lowest-sanction GP in every year, with Rs 0 recorded, while the other sampled GPs have sanctioned amounts on file; Govindapur, the next lowest overall, has Rs 99.78 lakh. Sanction data exist for only about one activity in six, so the result may reflect missing or unlinked records rather than an absence of approvals. The block should verify Chikilli’s sanction registers and link any missing sanctions to the relevant activities.
===FINDING 21===
LEAD: Spending under grant components classified as “Other” totals Rs 1.02 crore, or 3.6% of General-category voucher spending, and remains the smallest component in every year. Untied and tied components account for most of the recorded spending.
DETAIL: Untied spending is Rs 16.75 crore and tied spending Rs 10.71 crore, compared with Rs 1.02 crore under components outside those recognised groups. The low share is not itself a performance concern, but “Other” should be reviewed to confirm that component codes are valid and that tied or untied expenditure has not been misclassified.
===FINDING 22===
LEAD: Recorded statuses appear heavily backlogged: 10,108 of 12,704 activities, or 79.6%, remain marked “Activity Approved,” while only 17 are marked completed. A further 2,110 activities are recorded as ongoing.
DETAIL: “Activity Approved” and “Work Ongoing” are the two largest status groups in every year covered; 420 activities are marked abandoned. Officials should review older activities first and reconcile recorded status with payments, work progress and photo evidence. The 13 rows incorrectly carrying “Buildings” as a status should also be corrected.

DETAIL: A repeating pattern appears in the monthly and quarterly views, but not in fiscal-year totals.
